agenda.Text:
* The agenda: =orgs agenda=

  Three months of calendar, today's entries, and the week underneath. =,= and
  =.= step a day, =n= comes back to today, =t= changes the keyword of the
  entry under the cursor, =m= opens the month.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-agenda.png]]

* Agenda views: =orgs agenda -view=

  Org's custom agenda commands: a view is sections shown one after another (a
  day or a week of the agenda, open tasks with some keywords, a match, a
  search, stuck projects). Org's own =a=, =t=, =n= and =#= are built in; more
  come from =agenda: views:= in the yaml or from worg, where each person keeps
  their own. =orgs agenda -views= lists them, and =-as html= or =-as ics=
  prints one for a page or a calendar.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-agenda-view.png]]

  The hooks (=orgs hooks=), the phone's calendar (=orgs dav=) and the
  language server (=orgs lsp=) have their pictures in their own guides.

cols.Text:
* Column view: =orgs cols=

  org's column view of a file, from its =#+COLUMNS:= line. Parents total the
  columns that ask for it (=%EFFORT{:}=), enter edits a value in place, =s=
  sorts within each parent.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-cols.png]]

dash.Text:
* The day at a glance: =orgs dash=

  One screen that answers "what does today want from me": the agenda, the
  clock, the focus timer, the habits, the inbox and your watches, read
  together. It only reads; each card names the command that acts on it.
  =orgs dash -w= keeps it on screen, redrawn as things change, and
  =orgs dash -json= gives every card as data.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-dash.png]]

  A card whose part of the server is missing or broken says so in one dim
  line, and the others still draw.

dnd.Text:
* Dnd

  The =dnd= command is the client side of the D&D character module. It talks to
  the server over the =/dnd/*= REST API, so the rules, the ruleset modules and
  the character sheet renderers all live on the server.

  #+BEGIN_SRC bash
  orgs dnd new                          # guided character creation
  orgs dnd new -level 3 -name Lyra      # with a head start
  orgs dnd random -level 5 -out npc.org # roll a whole character
  orgs dnd list classes                 # browse a ruleset
  orgs dnd info -kind class -id wizard  # read one entry in full
  orgs dnd characters                   # every sheet the server knows about
  orgs dnd show -file lyra.org          # print a sheet in the terminal
  orgs dnd sheet -file lyra.org -format pdf -out lyra.pdf
  orgs dnd levelup -file lyra.org       # take the level you just earned
  orgs dnd refresh -file lyra.org       # recompute after hand editing
  orgs dnd rulesets                     # what content is loaded
  orgs dnd import -ddb 12345678         # bring a character over from d&d beyond
  #+END_SRC

  =orgs dnd new= walks you through creation the way a character builder does:
  every prompt lists the valid choices with a one line summary, marks the ones
  that suit your class with a star, and lets you ask for the full rules text,
  roll the choice randomly, or step back to change your mind.

  On a wide enough terminal the chooser is drawn in two panes: the list on the
  left, and the full rules text of whatever the cursor is on - the spell, item,
  feat or feature - on the right, so you can read before you commit. When a
  question takes several answers the header keeps a running count of what you
  have ticked ("selected 1 of 2") along with their names, and if you confirm the
  wrong number the list comes back with your picks still selected so you only
  have to correct them.

  Long lists are filtered by typing. The match is fuzzy on the name of an
  option, so =eldbl= finds Eldritch Blast, and a plain word also matches the
  summary beside it, so =fire= finds the spells that only mention it. The
  filter is editable: backspace takes a character off and the list widens
  again, =ctrl+w= takes a word, and escape clears it. The count beside the
  question says how much of the list you are looking at.

** Importing from D&D Beyond

  =orgs dnd import= converts a character you already have on D&D Beyond into an
  org character sheet, the same sheet =orgs dnd new= writes.

  #+BEGIN_SRC bash
  orgs dnd import -ddb https://www.dndbeyond.com/characters/12345678
  orgs dnd import -ddb 12345678 -out characters/lyra.org -force
  orgs dnd import -ddb 12345678 -preview      # convert and print, write nothing
  orgs dnd import -json saved.json            # from a payload you saved yourself
  orgs dnd import -forget                     # clear the saved session cookie
  #+END_SRC

  D&D Beyond has no login api, so a character whose privacy is set to public
  imports with no credential at all, and a private one asks for the
  =CobaltSession= cookie your browser is already holding - the prompt says where
  to find it. The cookie is traded for a short lived token by D&D Beyond's own
  auth service and can be kept in your system keyring so you are only asked
  once; it is never sent to your orgs server, which only ever sees the
  character json. =-cookie= and the =ORGS_DDB_COBALT= environment variable pass
  it in without a prompt for scripting.

  Everything is matched onto your ruleset by name, and anything that does not
  match - a subclass from a book the srd does not carry, a homebrew item - is
  still written onto the sheet under its own name and listed afterwards as
  something to check, so nothing is quietly dropped. Importing over a sheet
  that is already there keeps that sheet's identity and its inventory history,
  which D&D Beyond has no equivalent of.

  The appearance questions - age, height, weight, eyes, skin and hair - come
  with suggestions drawn from your race and your class, so a hill dwarf druid
  is offered warm hazel eyes and leaf tangled hair, and a tiefling warlock is
  offered eyes that are a solid orb of colour. You can still type your own, but
  it has to make sense: heights and weights are read in either imperial or
  metric and have to land somewhere your race could plausibly be, and a colour
  has to be a word rather than a number.

drill.Text:
* Flashcards: =orgs drill=

  Spaced repetition over your notes, org-drill style: the same cards, the same
  algorithms, the same =DRILL_*= properties. See [[*Flashcards — drilling your notes, org-drill style][Flashcards]] for how to write
  cards.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-drill.png]]

* Drill

  =orgs drill= drills a deck of flashcards at the command line: the decks of
  worg's Flashcards tab, the same cards, the same scheduling. Ratings are
  written by the server into the cards' =DRILL_*= properties, org-drill's
  way, so a deck can be drilled here, in worg and with Emacs' =org-drill= by
  turns. The user guide is =docs/drill.org=.

  #+BEGIN_SRC bash
  orgs drill                          # pick a deck, drill it
  orgs drill Spanish                  # a deck by name (or the start of one)
  orgs drill Spanish -cram            # everything not seen in 12 hours; nothing rescheduled
  orgs drill -q 'HasTags("drill")'    # any query, without saving a deck
  orgs drill Spanish -max 10 -minutes 5   # a shorter session than the deck's
  orgs drill -resume                  # carry on where q left off
  orgs drill ls                       # the decks and what each has due
  orgs drill stats Spanish            # one deck at a glance
  orgs drill cards Spanish            # every card: status, next review, ease, failures
  #+END_SRC

  =ls=, =stats= and =cards= take =-json= and =-format= for scripts; drilling
  needs a person at a terminal.

** The screen

   Across the top is org-drill's prompt line: the time so far, the card's
   status letter (=N= new, =Y= young, =o= old, =!= overdue, =F= failed, =C=
   cram) and how many are done, failed, mature and new. Under it, a rule shows
   how far through the session's limit you are.

   The card is drawn the way =orgs pres= draws a slide: tables, source blocks
   and pictures as they are written, in a slide theme's colours (=-theme=).
   Hidden clozes show as =[...]= or =[hint...]=; in the answer they are bold.

   | Key          | Question                   | Answer                       |
   |--------------+----------------------------+------------------------------|
   | space, any   | show the answer            |                              |
   | =0= - =5=    |                            | rate it; each button says when the card comes back |
   | =e=          | edit the card in =$EDITOR= | edit the card                |
   | =s=          | skip it                    |                              |
   | =?=          |                            | what the ratings mean        |
   | ↑ ↓ PgUp PgDn | scroll a tall card        | scroll                       |
   | =q=, esc     | stop                       | stop                         |

   A failed card comes back later in the session until you pass it. At the end
   you get org-drill's report, and its warning if too much was failed; *k*
   keeps going on what is left.

   =q= saves where you were, and =orgs drill -resume= carries on - reading the
   cards again, in case you edited them. Editing a card with =e= reads it again
   when the editor closes, so the card asked is the card as it now reads.

   A deck that asks for typed answers (in worg's deck settings) has a line to
   type into before the answer is shown, and your answer is shown beside it.

gantt.Text:
* Schedules: =orgs gantt=

  A saved query drawn as a gantt chart, the same plan worg draws: =EFFORT=
  sizes a bar, =AFTER= and =ORDERED= chain them, weekends are skipped, and
  =-crit= marks the critical path.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-gantt.png]]

habits.Text:
* Habits: =orgs habits=

  Every habit's last month at a glance: =█= kept, =░= missed, =·= not due.
  =orgs habits done <name>= ticks one off.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-habits.png]]

help.Text:
* Finding your way: =orgs help=

  Everything the command line can do is described by the binary itself, so
  the help always matches the version you are running. It needs no server.

  | You type                          | You get                                                                   |
  |-----------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
  | =orgs help=                       | every command, grouped by what it is for, in the order worth reading      |
  | =orgs help standup=               | one command: what it does, its flags, examples and what the guides say     |
  | =orgs help stand=                 | no such command, so the names it might have meant (=standup=)              |
  | =orgs help -all=                  | every command with every flag, one after another, for searching           |
  | =orgs help -json=                 | the command list as a table (name, group, usage), for a script            |
  | =orgs help -man search=           | a command's man page (roff); with no command, =orgs(1)=                    |
  | =orgs help -man-dir DIR=          | =orgs.1= and an =orgs-<command>.1= for every command, written into =DIR= |
  | =orgs completion zsh=             | tab completion for your shell                                             |

  A command's page reads top to bottom like this:

  [[file:docs/images/cli-help.png]]

  Some ways to use it:

  #+BEGIN_SRC sh
  # Which command has a flag for this?
  orgs help -all | grep -B20 -- '-since' | grep '^orgs '

  # Read a long page in a pager (search has the whole query language)
  orgs help search | less -R

  # Real man pages: write them once, then `man orgs-search`
  orgs help -man-dir ~/.local/share/man/man1

  # The list for a launcher or a wrapper script
  orgs help -json | jq -r '.[] | "\(.Name)\t\(.Usage)"'
  #+END_SRC

  Commands you add yourself show up too: every filter in your yaml is a
  command, listed under its own group (or "Other"). =orgs p= is the same list
  as a fuzzy picker, together with your saved queries and aliases.

kanban.Text:
* Boards: =orgs kanban=

  worg's kanban boards, the same boards, editable from the terminal. =H= and
  =L= move a card between columns (which changes its keyword), =J= and =K=
  reorder it, =t= picks a keyword, =c= clocks in.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-kanban.png]]

list.Text:
* Checklists: =orgs list=

  Every heading with =- [ ]= boxes in its own text is a list, wherever it
  lives, so a list refiled out of the inbox is still found, and so are the
  boxes under a task. =orgs list= picks one and works on it; =orgs list ls=
  draws them all, the way taskbook draws its boards.

  #+BEGIN_SRC sh
  orgs list                          # pick a list, then tick, add, edit, delete
  orgs list new Packing for Oslo     # a new list, filed under Checklists in the inbox
  orgs list ls -open                 # only lists with something left to do
  orgs list check -l groceries 3 4   # tick items 3 and 4
  #+END_SRC

  [[file:docs/images/cli-list.png]]

lsp.From: Editing :: Org files in any editor: =orgs lsp=
lsp.Text:
* Org files in any editor: =orgs lsp=
** What it is

  =orgs lsp= is a language server: any editor that speaks the Language Server
  Protocol - Neovim, Helix, Zed, Sublime Text, Emacs (eglot), the JetBrains
  IDEs, VS Code - gets these for org files from it:

  - *Completion*: TODO keywords after the stars (the file's =#+TODO:=, else
    the server's), tags after a heading's colon (this file's first, then every
    tag the server knows), link targets after =[[= - headings, =#custom-id=s,
    =<<targets>>=, =file:= with every org file, =file:x.org::*= with that
    file's headings, and =id:= with every heading that has an ID, found by its
    title - =#+= keywords and blocks, source block languages and property
    names.
  - *Go to definition* on a link: =[[*Heading]]=, =[[#id]]=, =[[target]]=,
    =[[file:x.org::*Heading]]=, =[[file:x.org::42]]= and =[[id:...]]=, which
    the server finds in whichever file has it.
  - *Clickable links* for urls, files and the =linkProtocols= in your yaml.
  - *The outline* (document symbols): headings with their keyword, tags and
    date, and named blocks and tables under the heading they are in; and every
    heading of every file as a workspace symbol.
  - *Folding* of headings, blocks and drawers.
  - *Diagnostics*: a block with no =#+END_=, a drawer with no =:END:=, a link
    to a heading, file or id that is not there, and the Harper or LanguageTool
    lints of =orgs lint=, whose suggestions are quick fixes.
  - *Code actions*: schedule, deadline, refile (recent targets first), archive,
    and run the source block, =#+CALL:= or inline code under the cursor - with
    a =▶ Run= lens over every block the server would run.

  In VS Code (Org Everywhere starts it for you): broken links, an unclosed
  drawer and an unclosed block in the Problems panel, and a hover on one.

  [[file:docs/images/lsp-vscode.png]]

  The outline, folding and the links within a file work with no server. The
  rest is one request each to =orgs serve=, as for every other command.

** Setting an editor up

  The server is =orgs lsp= on standard input and output. Its flags:
  =-lint auto|harper|languagetool|all|off= (default =auto=, the first checker
  the server offers), =-lang=, =-dialect=, =-ignore RULES=, =-refile-depth N=
  and =-path-map SERVER=LOCAL= for a server on another machine. The same can
  be sent as initialization options: =lint=, =lang=, =dialect=, =ignore=,
  =refileDepth=, =pathMap= (an object).

*** Neovim

   #+BEGIN_SRC lua
   vim.lsp.config('orgs', { cmd = { 'orgs', 'lsp' }, filetypes = { 'org' }, root_markers = { '.git' } })
   vim.lsp.enable('orgs')
   #+END_SRC

*** Helix (=languages.toml=)

   #+BEGIN_SRC toml
   [language-server.orgs]
   command = "orgs"
   args = ["lsp"]

   [[language]]
   name = "org"
   scope = "source.org"
   file-types = ["org"]
   language-servers = ["orgs"]
   #+END_SRC

*** Emacs (eglot)

   #+BEGIN_SRC emacs-lisp
   (add-to-list 'eglot-server-programs '(org-mode . ("orgs" "lsp")))
   #+END_SRC

*** Zed, Sublime Text, JetBrains

   Any "custom language server" setting that takes a command: =orgs lsp=, for
   files ending =.org=.

** How edits are made

  An editor holds text the server has not seen yet. So *schedule*, *deadline*
  and *run* send the buffer to the server, which makes the edit it would make
  to the file and sends back the text; the difference arrives as one edit
  you can undo, and the file on disk is not touched. Nothing needs saving
  first.

  *Refile* and *archive* change two files, so they work on the files: they
  refuse while the buffer has unsaved changes ("save first"), and afterwards
  bring the buffer up to what the server wrote if the editor did not reload
  it by itself.

  The commands behind the actions can be bound to keys with
  =workspace/executeCommand=, which is also how to schedule for a date the
  menu does not offer:

  | Command        | Arguments                    | Notes                                                  |
  |----------------+------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------|
  | =orgs.date=    | uri, line, name, value?      | =SCHEDULED=/=DEADLINE=; value as =orgs sched= reads it |
  | =orgs.run=     | uri, line                    | needs =babel.enable=                                   |
  | =orgs.refile=  | uri, line, {Filename, Olp}?  | asks where when the target is left out                 |
  | =orgs.archive= | uri, line                    |                                                        |

  #+BEGIN_SRC lua
  -- Neovim: schedule the heading under the cursor for Friday
  vim.lsp.buf.execute_command({ command = 'orgs.date',
    arguments = { vim.uri_from_bufnr(0), vim.fn.line('.') - 1, 'SCHEDULED', 'fri' } })
  #+END_SRC

plan.Text:
* Planning the day: =orgs plan=

  The day as hours: what is booked, what is free, and the tasks waiting for a
  slot, most urgent first. It is the agenda's day planner in worg, at a prompt.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-plan.png]]

pres.Text:
* Pres

  =orgs pres= gives an org file as a slideshow in the terminal: the deck worg's
  Presentations tab shows through reveal.js, drawn in box characters, colour and
  half-block pictures, for the talk given over ssh, in tmux beside the code, or
  from a laptop with no browser worth trusting on the projector.

  #+BEGIN_SRC bash
  orgs pres talk.org                  # present it
  orgs pres talk.org -presenter       # in a second terminal: notes, next slide, time
  orgs pres talk.org -theme linen     # any slide theme; builtin and term too
  orgs pres talk.org -at 12           # start on slide 12
  orgs pres talk.org -print | less -R # every slide, every step, printed
  orgs pres talk.org -json            # the outline, for a program
  orgs pres -list-themes
  #+END_SRC

  A name that is not a path is looked for in the configured org directories, and
  no server is needed: the file is read where you are.

** The deck

   The same rules as the html presentation exporters, because it is the same
   code deciding them:

   - =#+SLIDE_LEVEL: 2= makes level-2 headlines the slides and level-1 headlines
     the sections; a section with nothing of its own is drawn as a divider in
     large type. Without it every headline is a slide.
   - =#+TITLE:=, =#+SUBTITLE:=, =#+AUTHOR:=, =#+DATE:= and anything written
     above the first headline make the title page.
   - Speaker notes - a =:NOTES:= drawer, a =#+begin_notes= block, or a child
     heading called Notes - never reach the slide.
   - =:noexport:= or =:noslide:= leaves a heading out.
   - =:FRAGMENT: t= on a slide reveals its top-level list one item at a time;
     =#+ATTR_SLIDE: :frag= above any element makes that element a step.
   - =:BACKGROUND: #f4efe4= colours one slide, and its text turns light or dark
     to suit, as in the browser.
   - =:ALIGN: center= centres a slide; =:TRANSITION: fade= changes how it arrives.

   Settings are read with the presentation ladder: a slide's =:TERM_FOO:=, its
   =:SLIDE_FOO:=, its =:FOO:=, then the document's =#+TERM_FOO:= and
   =#+SLIDE_FOO:=. The =TERM_= forms are for this renderer only.

   | Setting               | Meaning                                       | Default  |
   |-----------------------+-----------------------------------------------+----------|
   | =#+SLIDE_THEME:=      | palette, from =templates/slides_theme_*.css=  | built in |
   | =#+TERM_TRANSITION:=  | =slide=, =fade= or =none=                     | slide    |
   | =#+TERM_WIDTH:=       | widest a column of text gets                  | 88       |
   | =#+TERM_FOOTER: nil=  | no footer or progress rule                    | shown    |

   A theme is the same file the html decks use: its =--slide-bg=, =--slide-ink=,
   =--slide-accent= and the rest become the terminal's colours, and its
   =@hljs:= style picks the nearest code colouring. =term= uses the terminal's
   own colours, for transparent terminals.

** What is drawn

   Paragraphs with bold, italic, underline, strike, =code=, links, sub- and
   superscripts (H_{2}O as H₂O) and smart dashes; lists with checkboxes;
   tables in a rounded box with columns of numbers right-aligned; source blocks
   coloured by language, with line numbers for =-n=; quotes, verse, centred
   text, special blocks (=#+begin_tip=) as labelled cards; footnotes at the foot
   of their slide; and pictures (png, jpeg, gif) in half blocks, with their
   =#+CAPTION:=. An svg or a web image is drawn as a labelled frame.

   A slide too tall for the terminal gives up its blank lines first, then
   scrolls with the arrow keys; a marker says there is more.

** Keys

   | Key                      | Does                                      |
   |--------------------------+-------------------------------------------|
   | → space l PgDn ⏎         | next step, or next slide                  |
   | ← h PgUp ⌫               | back                                      |
   | N P                      | next or previous slide, skipping steps    |
   | ↓ ↑ j k                  | scroll a slide too tall for the screen    |
   | g G                      | first or last slide                       |
   | 12 then ⏎                | slide 12                                  |
   | o tab                    | every slide, to pick from                 |
   | n                        | speaker notes under the slide             |
   | t r                      | show the timer, restart it                |
   | f                        | footer and progress rule                  |
   | T                        | next theme                                |
   | b .                      | black screen                              |
   | e                        | edit this slide in =$EDITOR=              |
   | R                        | reload now                                |
   | ? q                      | keys, quit                                |

   The file is reloaded whenever it is saved, keeping your place, so a deck can
   be written in one window and watched in another.

** Presenting with two windows

   =orgs pres talk.org -presenter= in a second terminal shows the speaker's
   view: this slide's notes, the step you are on, what comes next, the time
   since you started and the clock. The two windows follow each other, and
   either can drive.

protocol.From: Setup :: org-protocol: capture from the browser
protocol.Text:
* =orgs protocol=

  #+BEGIN_SRC sh
  orgs protocol install        # handle org-protocol:// links (macOS, Linux, Windows)
  orgs protocol status         # which program handles them now
  orgs protocol uninstall
  orgs protocol bookmarklets -temp Web
  orgs protocol links          # what store-link has kept, newest first
  orgs protocol 'org-protocol://capture?url=…'   # what a click runs
  #+END_SRC

  - *macOS*: a small applet, =~/Applications/Orgs Protocol.app=, made with
    =osacompile= and registered with Launch Services as the default handler.
    If Emacs Client handled these links before, it no longer does;
    =uninstall= gives them back. What a click prints goes to
    =~/Library/Caches/orgs/protocol.log=.
  - *Linux*: =~/.local/share/applications/orgs-protocol.desktop=, made the
    default with =xdg-mime=.
  - *Windows*: =HKCU\Software\Classes\org-protocol=. orgs is a console
    program, so a window flashes up on each click.

  The handler runs this binary with this config file, so it talks to the
  server and uses the login the install was made with. When it runs from a
  click, a problem shows as a desktop notification.

recap.Text:
* The week in review: =orgs recap=

  A week or a month on one page: what was finished, where the time went, how
  the habits held up, words written and what is still blocked. Like
  =orgs standup= it is Slack's markup unless you ask for =-md=.

  #+BEGIN_SRC sh
  orgs recap                        # the last seven days
  orgs recap -last -week            # last week, Monday to Sunday
  orgs recap -month                 # this month so far
  orgs recap -from 2026-10-01 -to 2026-10-15
  orgs recap -block 2026-Q3 -md     # a clock table range, as Markdown
  #+END_SRC

  [[file:docs/images/cli-recap.png]]

review.Text:
* The weekly review: =orgs review=

  Everything that wants a decision: projects with nothing to do next, deadlines
  nobody scheduled, things waiting on somebody else, time booked against open
  tasks. =orgs review -fix= walks them one at a time.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-review.png]]

search.Text:
* Asking questions: =orgs search=

  The same query language worg's Search tab uses. Plain words match headlines;
  an expression can ask anything the database knows.

  #+BEGIN_SRC sh
  orgs search 'IsTask() && HasTags("work")'
  orgs search 'DeadlineWithin("7d")' -json | jq '.[].Headline'
  #+END_SRC

  [[file:docs/images/cli-search.png]]

snip.Text:
* Snip

  =orgs snip= keeps the command lines worth keeping - and finds the ones you
  wrote down and forgot - in your org files. It does what [[https://github.com/knqyf263/pet][pet]]
  does, with org source blocks for snippets: a heading says what the command
  does, its tags file it, the block is the command. Every shell block in your
  notes is a snippet, so a command written into a project's notes months ago
  turns up beside the ones saved on purpose.

  #+BEGIN_SRC bash
  orgs snip                          # find one, fill in its parameters, run it
  orgs snip docker logs              # start the search on those words
  orgs snip print [words]            # print it instead (what the shell key uses)
  orgs snip copy [words]             # put it on the clipboard
  orgs snip run backup -set dest=/mnt -y   # no questions: for scripts and cron
  orgs snip new 'rsync -av <src> <dest=/backup>'   # save one
  orgs snip ls -t docker             # list, by tag (comma separated: any of them)
  orgs snip show [words]             # what it is and what it asks for
  orgs snip edit [words]             # open it where it is written
  orgs snip shell zsh                # the ctrl-s key and snip-prev
  #+END_SRC

** A snippet

   #+BEGIN_SRC org
   ,* Docker                                                     :docker:
   ,** Tail a container's logs
   ,#+begin_src bash
   docker logs -f --tail <lines=100> <container=web>
   ,#+end_src
   #+END_SRC

   Any =sh=, =bash=, =zsh= or =fish= block is a snippet (=-all= takes every
   language). Its title is its heading, plus its =#+NAME:= when it has one; its
   tags are its heading's and the ones it inherits. A =:dir= header argument is
   where it runs. Its last =#+RESULTS:= is shown beside it.

** Parameters

   | Written                          | Means                                              |
   |----------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------|
   | =<name>=                         | a value to fill in                                 |
   | =<name=default>=                 | with a default (an === in it is fine)              |
   | =<flags?>=                       | optional: left empty, it is left out               |
   | =\<b>=                           | a literal =<b>=, not a parameter                   |
   | =:var host="db.internal"=        | babel's way: a parameter where the body says =$host= |
   | =:var env='("dev" "prod")=       | babel's way, with choices                          |

   A choice is written as pet writes it, and the first is the default:

   #+BEGIN_SRC sh
   kubectl -n <ns=|_dev_||_staging_||_prod_|> get pods
   #+END_SRC

   The =:var= form keeps the block runnable with =C-c C-c= in Emacs. A name
   used twice is one parameter.

   Values are quoted for the shell as much as where they land needs: inside the
   command's own quotes they are escaped for those quotes; elsewhere a value is
   single-quoted only if it has a space or something the shell would act on.
   A glob or a =$VAR= in a value is left alone, because that is somebody asking
   for one.

** The form

   With parameters to fill in, a form shows the finished command - redrawn as
   you type, values in colour - above a field for each one, defaults already
   in. *Tab* and *shift-tab* move between fields, *↑ ↓* cycle a choice,
   *ctrl-u* clears, *enter* runs (or prints, or copies), *esc* cancels and runs
   nothing. =-set name=value= fills one in without asking.

   A snippet with no parameters is shown and asked about before it runs;
   =-y= skips the question. Commands run here, in your shell - never on the
   server.

** The picker

   Snippets you used recently come first. The pane shows the command coloured,
   its parameters and defaults, where it runs and what it last printed.
   *enter* does what the command was asked to do; *ctrl-p* prints, *ctrl-y*
   copies, *ctrl-e* edits, *ctrl-/* hides the pane.

** Saving one

   #+BEGIN_SRC bash
   orgs snip new 'du -ah <dir=.> | sort -rh | head -n <count=20>'   # asks what it does, and tags
   orgs snip new -d 'Find big files' -t disk,find 'du -ah ...'      # asks nothing
   pbpaste | orgs snip new -d 'From the clipboard'                   # the command on stdin
   orgs snip new                                                     # type it, several lines if need be
   #+END_SRC

   It is filed under "Snippets" in =snippets.org= in your first org directory,
   through the server's built-in =Snippet= capture template - which is also in
   worg's capture dialog and =orgs cap=. Define a capture template of your own
   called =Snippet= to file them somewhere else. A command already saved is
   refused (=-force= saves it again).

** In your shell

   #+BEGIN_SRC bash
   eval "$(orgs snip shell zsh)"      # in ~/.zshrc
   eval "$(orgs snip shell bash)"     # in ~/.bashrc
   orgs snip shell fish | source      # in config.fish
   #+END_SRC

   *ctrl-s* opens the picker on what you have typed so far and puts the chosen
   command, filled in, on your command line - to edit, run, and keep in your
   history like anything you typed. =ORGS_SNIP_KEY= picks another key.
   =snip-prev= saves the command you just ran (=snip-prev -d 'what' -t tags=).

standup.Text:
* The morning standup: =orgs standup=

  What you did since the last working day (Friday, on a Monday), what is on
  today and what is in the way, written in Slack's markup so it can be pasted
  straight into a channel. =-copy= puts it on the clipboard as well, =-md=
  writes GitHub Markdown instead, =-since mon= starts from a day of your
  choosing and =-n= caps each section (the rest are counted).

  [[file:docs/images/cli-standup.png]]

  Every part is read by the view it comes from (the agenda, the clock table,
  the weekly review's waiting list, the dependency check), so a standup never
  says something the agenda would contradict.

tables.Text:
* Tables: =orgs tables=

  Every org table in your notes, in a picker with the table drawn beside it.
  =ctrl-e= runs its =#+TBLFM= formulas.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-tables.png]]

tui.Text:
* One screen for everything: =orgs tui=

  A query's results in a list, with the heading's body beside it. =:= changes
  the query, =/= filters what is there, =t= changes a keyword, enter opens the
  heading in your editor.

  [[file:docs/images/cli-tui.png]]

Querying:
* Overview

  Many operations in orgs require you to select the nodes that the operation applies to.
  - Agendas
  - Filtered Tabular Lists
  - Various Exporters
  - Etc

  Lots of these things require a filtered list of nodes to operate. Orgs does this through
  a node filter. This is an expression that is applied to nodes in the DB and returns only those
  nodes that pass the query.

  The most common expression starts with:

   #+BEGIN_SRC cpp
   !IsArchive() && IsTodo()
   #+END_SRC

   This will select all active nodes that have an active TODO status on them throughout all of your org mode files.
   Note the negation on IsArchive() these expressions support most common operators

   Agenda views will often add a date query:

   #+BEGIN_SRC cpp
   !IsArchive() && IsTodo() && OnDate('<specific date>')
   #+END_SRC

   People who follow GTD will often want lists that follow the common patterns:

   #+BEGIN_SRC cpp
   !IsArchive() && IsProject()
   !IsArchive() && IsTodo() && IsStatus('NEXT')
   !IsArchive() && IsTodo() && ( IsStatus('WAITING') || IsStatus('BLOCKED') )
   #+END_SRC

   This represents some of your common lists that you need to review regularly:
   - Projects List
   - Next Actions List
   - Waiting On List


** Orgs Expression Methods Reference

  A second way to write a query, for typing into a search box. It is turned
  into the full expression on the server, so it can ask everything the full
  form can ask through the functions above, and the two can be used anywhere
  a query is taken.

  #+BEGIN_SRC sh
  orgs search 'NEXT :work:'
  orgs search 'todo due:<3d -:home:'
  orgs search 'project stuck | WAITING old:>14'
  #+END_SRC

  - Words side by side must all match; =|= (or =or=) means either.
  - =-= (or =not=) in front of a term turns it round; brackets group.
  - Archived headings are left out unless the query says =archived=.
  - A plain word, ="quoted phrase"= or =/regex/= searches headlines. Words and
    phrases match anywhere and ignore case; a regex is used as written.

  | Term                          | Means                                       |
  |-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------|
  | =todo= =done= =task= =project= | IsTodo IsDone IsTask IsProject             |
  | =next= =stuck= =habit= =missed= | IsNextTask IsBlockedProject IsHabit MissedHabit |
  | =archived= =record= =collection= | IsArchived IsRecord IsCollection         |
  | =tagged= =untagged=           | has tags / NoTags                           |
  | =scheduled= =deadline= =dated= | HasScheduled HasDeadline HasAnyDate        |
  | =clocked= =linked= =broken= =orphan= | HasClock HasLinks HasBrokenLinks, no backlinks |
  | =checklist= =table= =drawer= =block= | HasChecklist HasTable HasDrawer HasBlock |
  | =NEXT= (any word in capitals) | IsStatus("NEXT")                            |
  | =:work:= =:work:urgent:=      | HasTags("work") - every tag named           |
  | =:/^M[0-9]+$/:=               | HasTagMatching                              |
  | =#A=                          | IsPriority("A")                             |
  | =due:past= =due:today= =due:<3d= =due:fri= | DeadlinePast, DeadlineWithin(0/3/days to friday) |
  | =due:any= =due:none=          | HasDeadline, !HasDeadline                   |
  | =sched:...=                   | the same for SCHEDULED                      |
  | =on:today= =on:fri= =on:2026-10-30= | OnDate                                |
  | =before:today= =after:fri= =before:-2w= | a SCHEDULED, DEADLINE or timestamp of its own before / after that day (DateBefore DateAfter) |
  | =old:>30= =old:<7=            | OlderThan(30), DaysOld under 7              |
  | =streak:>7= =backlinks:0= =left:>0= =items:>5= =age:<3= | HabitStreak BacklinkCount ChecklistLeft ChecklistCount DaysOld, compared |
  | =file:work= =in:contact= =record:contact= | InFile InCollection IsRecord     |
  | =group:WORK= =text:word= =title:word= =link:word= =tag:work= | InTagGroup MatchContent MatchHeadline LinksTo HasTags |
  | =status:next= =priority:a=    | IsStatus("NEXT") IsPriority("A")            |
  | =client:acme=                 | any other key is a property: MatchProperty("CLIENT", ...) |
  | =client:*=                    | HasProperty("CLIENT")                       |
  | =effort:<2h= =level:>=2= =scheduled:<<+1w>= | PropCompare("EFFORT", "<", "2h"): =<= =<== =>= =>== ===, =!== |
  | ={{ WorkTasks }}=             | a yaml filter, as in the full form          |

  Org's own match strings work too, as an agenda's tags search writes them:
  =+work-boss+PRIORITY="A"|urgent=, =work/NEXT|WAITING=, =+project/!=,
  =Effort<2:00=, =CATEGORY={^cli}=, =SCHEDULED<="<+1w>"/-DONE=. One is told
  from a short query by having no spaces and starting with =+= or =-= or using
  one of === =<= =>= =/= ={= =&=.

  A query is read as the full form when it calls a function (=IsTodo()=) or
  uses =&&= or =||=, so every query written before keeps its meaning.
  =orgs search -explain= prints the full form a short query becomes.

QueryFuncs.BacklinkCount: how many links point at this heading, as a number to compare: BacklinkCount() == 0 finds the orphans
QueryFuncs.ChecklistCount: how many checkboxes the node's own text has, as a number to compare
QueryFuncs.ChecklistDone: returns true if the node has checkboxes and every one is ticked
QueryFuncs.ChecklistLeft: how many of the node's checkboxes are still open, as a number to compare
QueryFuncs.DateAfter: DateAfter("2026 30 10") is true when one of those dates falls on a day after it; a range counts by its end
QueryFuncs.DateBefore: DateBefore("2026 30 10") (year, day, month, as OnDate) is true when the node's SCHEDULED, DEADLINE or an active timestamp of its own falls on a day before that one
QueryFuncs.DaysOld: how many days ago the node's newest date (SCHEDULED, DEADLINE, CLOSED or timestamp) was, as a number to compare; -1 with no date
QueryFuncs.DeadlinePast: returns true if the DEADLINE is before today: overdue, where a deadline of today is only due
QueryFuncs.DeadlineWithin: DeadlineWithin(N) is true when the DEADLINE falls between today and N days ahead, in calendar days
QueryFuncs.HabitStreak: how many times in a row a habit has been kept, as a number to compare: IsHabit() && HabitStreak() > 7; 0 once the run is broken
QueryFuncs.HasAStatus: returns true if a node has a valid status
QueryFuncs.HasAnyDate: returns true if the node has a SCHEDULED date, a DEADLINE or a timestamp
QueryFuncs.HasBacklinks: returns true when something else links at this heading; HasBacklinks(2) asks for at least two
QueryFuncs.HasBlock: Checks if the node contains a block object.
QueryFuncs.HasBrokenLinks: returns true when a link under this heading resolves to nothing
QueryFuncs.HasChecklist: returns true if the node's own text has checkboxes
QueryFuncs.HasClock: returns true if time has ever been clocked against the node
QueryFuncs.HasDeadline: returns true if the node has a DEADLINE
QueryFuncs.HasDrawer: Checks if the node contains a drawer.
QueryFuncs.HasLinks: returns true when this heading links out at all
QueryFuncs.HasProperty: Returns true if the headline has the specific property
QueryFuncs.HasScheduled: returns true if the node has a SCHEDULED date
QueryFuncs.HasTable: Checks if the node contains a table.
QueryFuncs.HasTagMatching: returns true if any tag on the node, its parents or the file matches a regular expression: HasTagMatching("^M[0-9]+$")
QueryFuncs.HasTags: returns true if a node has any tags
QueryFuncs.HasTimestamp: returns true if the node has a plain timestamp of its own
QueryFuncs.InCollection: InCollection("contact") is true for anything filed in that collection - the records, the container, and anything written under it
QueryFuncs.InFile: InFile(REGEX) is true when the path of the node's file matches, its absolute path included: InFile("work")
QueryFuncs.InTagGroup: cheat, returns true if any tags in a tag group are applied to a node
QueryFuncs.InheritedProperty: =InheritedProperty("CLIENT")= or =InheritedProperty("CLIENT", "acme")=: the property set on this heading, one above it, or the file's =#+PROPERTY:= lines. =HasProperty= and =MatchProperty= inherit only the names =propertyInheritance= lists (=["*"]= for all), and =CATEGORY=.
QueryFuncs.IsActive: returns true if the status of a node is an active status (IE not DONE)
QueryFuncs.IsArchived: Check if a headline is in the archived state or not (in an archived file or has an ARCHIVE tag)
QueryFuncs.IsBlocked: An open task that cannot be marked done yet: a child heading is still open, or, under a parent with an =ORDERED= property, a sibling above it is (org's TODO dependencies; =:NOBLOCKING: t= is never blocked).
QueryFuncs.IsBlockedProject: Check if this is a project heading and it DOES NOT have a child marked NEXT.
QueryFuncs.IsCollection: returns true for the container heading a collection files its records under
QueryFuncs.IsDone: returns true if the node's keyword is a finished one (DONE and kin), by the keywords of its own file
QueryFuncs.IsHabit: returns true for a habit (a :STYLE: habit heading)
QueryFuncs.IsNextTask: Check if a headline has a NEXT action status. This is GTD support and uses the defaultNextStatus value and #+NEXT comment
QueryFuncs.IsPartOfProject: returns true if a task is a subnode of a project node
QueryFuncs.IsPriority: Check if the priority matches a specific value.
QueryFuncs.IsProject: returns true for nodes that are defined as a project (see project definition)
QueryFuncs.IsRecord: returns true for a record heading (anything with a RECORD property); IsRecord("contact") asks about one collection
QueryFuncs.IsStatus: returns true if a node has a given status
QueryFuncs.IsTask: Syntatical sugar for the following: "!IsArchived() && IsTodo() && !IsProject()"
QueryFuncs.IsTodo: returns true if a node has an active status (the same as IsActive currently)
QueryFuncs.LinksTo: LinksTo(REGEX) is true when a link under this heading points at something matching - the target as written, its description, or the file and headline it lands on
QueryFuncs.MatchContent: MatchContent(REGEX) runs an RE over the headline and the text under it
QueryFuncs.MatchHeadline: Run an RE against each headline and check for a match
QueryFuncs.MatchProperty: MatchProperty(NAME, REGEX) returns true if the property value matches the implied regex
QueryFuncs.MissedHabit: returns true when a habit has gone longer since it was last done than its repeater allows
QueryFuncs.NoTags: returns true if a node does not have any tags on it
QueryFuncs.OlderThan: OlderThan(N) is true when the node's newest date is at least N days ago; never true for a node with no date
QueryFuncs.OnDate: OnDate("2026 30 01") (year, day, month) is true when the heading lands on that day in the agenda: a timestamp, SCHEDULED or DEADLINE on it, a repeat of one, a range spanning it, and on today also an overdue SCHEDULED and a DEADLINE inside its warning period or past it (the rules of GET /agenda)
QueryFuncs.PropCompare: =PropCompare("EFFORT", "<", "2:00")=: a property's value against a value, as org's property match compares: as dates when the value is one (=<2026-11-01>=, =<today>=, =<+1w>=), as numbers when both are numbers, as durations (=2:30=, =2h=), else as text. Operators =<= =<== =>= =>== ===, =!==. The special properties =TODO=, =PRIORITY=, =LEVEL=, =ITEM=, =CATEGORY=, =TAGS=, =SCHEDULED=, =DEADLINE= and =CLOSED= work too. A heading without the property is only =!== anything.
QueryFuncs.ScheduledPast: returns true if the SCHEDULED date is before today (today itself is not past)
QueryFuncs.ScheduledWithin: ScheduledWithin(N) is true when the SCHEDULED date falls between today and N days ahead, in calendar days
QueryFuncs.ThisWeek: returns true if a node lands in the agenda on any day of the last seven, today included
QueryFuncs.Today: returns true if a node is scheduled for today
QueryFuncs.Yesterday: returns true if a node is scheduled for yesterday

log: orgs log                   a heading's clock entries
lsp: orgs lsp                        speak LSP on stdin and stdout
orgs lsp -lint off              without the spelling and grammar checkers
orgs lsp -lint all -lang en-GB  both checkers, British English
mcp: orgs mcp                    speak MCP on stdin and stdout
orgs mcp -read-only         offer only the tools that read
orgs mcp -list              what it would offer, and exit
mentions: orgs mentions Apollo                  where "Apollo" is written but not linked
orgs mentions Apollo -link            pick which of them become links (fzf, tab marks)
orgs mentions Apollo -link -only 1,3  link the first and third, no picker
orgs mentions Apollo -link -yes       link every one of them
orgs mentions -file notes.org -line 40   the heading line 40 is under
merge: orgs merge Rocket Booster            Booster (and its children) into Rocket
models: orgs models                         every runtime, its state, its models
orgs models suggested               what each runtime suggests pulling
orgs models pull qwen3:8b           fetch one (progress until it is done)
orgs models cancel <model>          stop a pull
orgs models delete <model>          asks first; -yes to not
note: orgs note 'rang back, no answer'    a line onto the body
notifications: orgs notifications              the list, newest first, unread marked
orgs notifications -unread      only those not yet read
orgs notifications -read        the list, then mark them all read
orgs notifications -follow      say each new one as it happens (ctrl-c ends)
notify: orgs notify status          what the server does: reminders, digest, quiet
orgs notify test            one notification through the server's own path
orgs notify test -here      one shown on this machine, no server involved
orgs notify listen          show the server's notifications on this machine
outline: orgs outline notes.org     the tree, which nothing else in the CLI showed
p: orgs p                 pick a command, a saved query, a filter or an alias
orgs p -print          print the chosen command line instead of running it
orgs p -json           the list, for a program
paste: orgs paste 'MatchHeadline("Q3 report")'   under that heading's body
orgs paste hOpOB7vIg6oiYz5sMVS=            under the heading with that hash
orgs paste -file notes.org -line 42        after line 42 (a table's last row)
orgs paste -file notes.org                 at the end of the file
orgs paste                                 keep it, print [[file:…]] to stdout
orgs paste -template todo                  …relative to where that capture goes
orgs paste -in chart.png 'IsProject()'     a file instead of the clipboard
plan: orgs plan                          today: the hours as a timeline, then what is left to place
orgs plan -date tomorrow           another day (any date `orgs sched` reads)
orgs plan report 10:00             put the task matching "report" at 10:00, for its EFFORT (else an hour)
orgs plan report 10:00-11:30       ... for exactly that long
orgs plan report next              ... in the first free gap long enough
orgs plan 10:00                    pick the task (fzf), then place it
orgs plan 'IsStatus("NEXT")' 14    a query or a hash names the task, as for every write verb
orgs plan unblock report           take it off the day (a repeating task keeps its date)
pres: orgs pres talk.org -presenter      the speaker's window: notes, next, time
orgs pres talk.org -theme linen    any slide theme, or builtin / term
orgs pres talk.org | less -R       every slide, printed
orgs pres talk.org -json           the outline, for a program
print: orgs print                         this week, a4 landscape, written to week-2026-10-12.html
orgs print day -from tomorrow -theme minimal -f pdf -open
prop: orgs prop EFFORT=2h                 the property drawer
protocol: orgs protocol 'org-protocol://capture?template=w&url=…'   what the system runs on a click
orgs protocol install          make orgs the handler for org-protocol:// links
orgs protocol uninstall        stop being it
orgs protocol status           which program handles them now
orgs protocol bookmarklets     bookmarklets for this server (-temp NAME)
orgs protocol links            the links store-link has kept, newest first
q: orgs q                      pick one and run it
orgs q stale                run the one called stale
orgs q ls                   what is saved
orgs q edit stale           change it in $EDITOR
orgs q watch stale          say when it finds something new (watch.go)
orgs q watches              what is being watched
orgs q stale -csv -out stale.csv   its headings as a spreadsheet (csvout)
orgs q watch blocked                  tell me when "blocked" finds something new
orgs q watch blocked -left -desktop   ...and when something leaves it, with a popup
rec: orgs rec                           every record there is
orgs rec ls -type equipment        one collection
orgs rec find thinkpad             the ones matching
orgs rec show thinkpad             one, in full
orgs rec add -type equipment       asked for, field by field
orgs rec fields -type equipment    what that collection uses
orgs rec collections               what is being kept
recap: orgs recap                    the last seven days
orgs recap -month             this month so far
orgs recap -last -week        last week, Monday to Sunday
refresh: orgs refresh                    everything on a timer: what, how often, last run, next, how it went
orgs refresh run 2              run the second of those now (or its key)
orgs refresh run due            whatever is due
orgs refresh dash.org           that file's dynamic blocks and table formulas, now
orgs refresh dash.org -blocks   and its :schedule source blocks
rename: orgs rename 'a better title'        the headline text
retag: orgs retag work job                  rename a tag everywhere (a merge when job exists)
orgs retag -delete stale             take a tag off everything
orgs retag work job -query 'IsProject()'   only the headlines a query matches
orgs retag work job -file a.org,b.org      only some files
review: orgs review                 everything that wants a decision
orgs review stale           just that check
orgs review -fix            walk them, and change them as you go
orgs review week            the weekly review wizard (week.go)
orgs review week            the seven steps, one at a time
orgs review week -restart   from the top, whatever step was left
orgs review week -days 14   waiting items older than a fortnight
orgs review week -json      what each step would ask about, as json
search:
orgs search 'IsStatus("NEXT") && OlderThan("30d")' -json \
  | jq -r .Hash | orgs tag +stale -
show: orgs show                       pick one and read it
orgs show 'IsStatus("NEXT")'    the first match, or a picker over them
orgs show -log                  with the clock entries
orgs show -raw                  the body text and nothing else
orgs show -edit                 open it where it lives
site: orgs site blog -out ./public                 the site, written here
orgs site blog -out ./public -theme journal  in another theme
orgs site blog -local -out /srv/www          written on the server's disk
snip: orgs snip shell fish | source     in config.fish
orgs snip                       find one, fill in its parameters, run it
orgs snip docker logs           the same, starting on those words
orgs snip print [words]         ... and print it instead (for a shell key)
orgs snip copy [words]          ... and put it on the clipboard
orgs snip run backup -set dest=/mnt -y     no questions, for scripts
orgs snip ls [-t docker]        list them
orgs snip edit [words]          open one where it is written
orgs snip shell zsh             the ctrl-s key and `snip-prev`, for your shell
split: orgs split Apollo                    a heading out to a file of its own
orgs split Apollo -to projects/      ... into a folder, or -to path/name.org
standup: orgs standup                  since the last working day (Friday, on a Monday)
orgs standup -since mon       from a day of your choosing
orgs standup -md -copy        GitHub Markdown, and onto the clipboard
stats: orgs stats                  keywords, tags, files, clocked time
tables: orgs tables                       pick one, with it drawn beside the list
orgs tables ls -file budget.org   one file's tables
orgs tables show expenses         one table, drawn
orgs tables eval expenses         run its formulas and write the result back
orgs tables ls -json              for a program to read
orgs tables import data.csv notes.org -header -name sales
tags: orgs tags                  the tag vocabulary, and what uses each one
tangle: orgs tangle notes.org      write the source blocks out as files
timer: orgs timer countdown 25      a count down; a notification when it ends
orgs timer set 0:10:00       as though it started that long ago
orgs timer note they agreed  "- 0:03:12 :: they agreed" under the clocked heading
orgs timer note -hash H ...  under that heading instead
timesheet: orgs timesheet -block thisweek -f pdf       this week's sittings, signed off
orgs timesheet -block 2026-10 -f csv        a row a sitting, for a spreadsheet
todo: orgs todo DONE                       a picker, when there is somebody to pick
orgs todo DONE 'IsStatus("NEXT")'    a query, the same language /search takes
orgs todo DONE hOpOB7vIg6oiYz5sMVS=  one heading, by hash
transclude: orgs transclude            whether it is on
orgs transclude on         on, and written into the server's yaml
orgs transclude ls notes.org   each #+transclude: line and where its text comes from
triage: orgs triage              each inbox item in turn: r refile, s schedule, t tag,
orgs triage -someday     the someday pile: k keep, p promote, s schedule,
tui: orgs tui 'IsTask() && Today()'    start on something else
orgs tui -query '{{ WorkTasks }}' a filter from the yaml
voice: orgs voice                     record until you press enter, then file it
orgs voice -on 'the migration' append to that heading instead
orgs voice -f take.m4a         a recording you already have
orgs voice ls                  what the server is holding
orgs voice rm <id>             throw one away
orgs voice config              what transcription is available
watch: orgs watch                          print each change as it happens
orgs watch -exec 'make notes'       run that when anything changes
orgs watch -kinds clockin,clockout  only the clock
orgs watch -once                    wait for one change and exit
orgs watch -json                    one json object per line, for a program
worg: orgs worg            the agenda, or whatever worg opens on
orgs worg Kanban     a view by the name worg switches on
orgs worg -print     the link instead of opening it
write: orgs write                      today against the goals, the streak, the last 14 days
orgs write -short               one line for a status bar: ✍ 412/500 · 6d
orgs write log -days 30         words per day, and the files they went into
orgs write goals                what they are
orgs write ideas                the idea generators
orgs write ideas character -n 3 -genre sf -set role=villain
orgs write snapshots draft.org  (or a heading) newest first
